extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and students/scholars of political anthropology, history, and sociology (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of how present‑making (gifts/oblations) evolves into institutionalized forms of revenue and maintenance (tribute, taxes, fees, salaries, ecclesiastical revenues) across societies and times. Draws on cross-cultural historical examples to trace mechanisms (periodicity, commutation, social meanings) behind the transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propitiatory presents develop into tribute and taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: From propitiatory presents, voluntary and exceptional to begin with, but becoming as political power strengthens less voluntary and more general, there eventually grow up universal and involuntary contributions — established tribute; and that with the rise of a currency this passes into taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with historical examples (Merovingian/Carolingian Europe, Persia, ancient Mexico/Peru, Tonga). Shows mechanism: voluntary offerings become regular (periodicity) and then compulsory; increasing political power converts extra‑voluntary gifts into extra‑involuntary dues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodicity and locality determine nature of tribute in kind
rubrics_metrics.description: When presents become regular in an extensive kingdom, they will represent the products of the respective districts; where arrangements are less settled, gifts from the same place are miscellaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ancient Peru (fragrant woods, cotton, emeralds, gold, parrots, honey, wax), ancient Mexico (fish, flesh, corn, cotton, gold). Early French towns gave 'oxen, sheep, wine, oats, game, wax‑torches, confections, horses, arms, vessels of gold and silver, etc.' The goods reflect local abundance and individual abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutation into money facilitates taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: As money‑values become more definite and payments in money become easier, commutation results (payments in money instead of goods), which facilitates the development of taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Carolingian 'inferencla' originally paid in cattle now in money; English towns giving money instead of goods to the king and his suite. The passage from tribute in kind to monetary payments accelerates fiscal regularization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular/extraordinary presents can become customary dues with social penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Usual presents (annual or festival offerings) may be regulated by usage such that to fall short is loss of office, and to exceed is increase of favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persian Nourouze examples: 'The first of these extra taxes may be termed usual and extraordinary presents. The usual presents to the king are those made annually ... The amount presented on this occasion is generally regulated by usage; to fall short is loss of office, and to exceed is increase of favor.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Presents to subordinate officials for services evolve into fees, bribes, and official revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Special presents made to state‑functionaries when called on to use their power (e.g., judicial aid) commonly become customary and later compulsory, forming part of officials' incomes; in later stages, such payments appear as fees or even bribery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chibchas required gifts before petitions; Sumatra chief with no revenue except payments for determining causes; Norman England: 'purchase' of royal writs originally a present; Blackstone's comment that writs became demandable on paying usual fees; modern parallels of poorly salaried officials requiring bribes as representatives of earlier present‑based maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presents to the dead and gods are analogous to presents to the living (oblations = presents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oblations (offerings to gods/ghosts) are at first literally presents; the things given and motives for giving them remain the same as presents to living rulers—food, drink, clothing, valuables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread ethnographic examples: food/drink left with corpses (Papuans, Tahitians, Mexicans), clothes periodically taken to graves (Esquimaux), large quantities of clothes for potentates' tombs (Congo), and libations for spirits. The essay emphasizes the original identity between offerings and presents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food and drink are the essential components of oblations and sacrificial practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Food and drink, the earliest propitiatory gifts to living persons and ghosts, remain everywhere the essential components of an oblation to a deity; temples are their houses, sacrifices their food, altars their tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows parallels across low and higher societies; cites Greek practice and biblical/Levitical rites. Also connects shared consumption (priests and votaries eating parts of offerings) as establishing bonds between worshippers and deity/priests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumption of offerings creates social bond and leads to priestly maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: When offerings are partly consumed by priests (or by the community together with the supernatural), a bond of union is established implying protection and allegiance; from such presents arises maintenance for priests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnographic examples: Kukis—priest eats sacrificed fowl; Bustar tribes—offerings become property of officiating priest; Dahomey and Ashantee—priests live on 'benevolences'/'moiety of offerings'; ancient Peru and Greece—sacrificial remains are priests' fees; early Church oblations becoming customary maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblations shift from voluntary gifts to customary/bequested ecclesiastical revenues
rubrics_metrics.description: Offertory contributions, voluntary in early times, became by continual payment dues by custom and eventually developed into fixed ecclesiastical revenues and sacred estates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracing development: Tertullian's 'deposita pietatis' (voluntary oblations) → medieval practices where presents were taken to bishops' houses → enlargements into bequests nominally to God but practically to the Church, forming church revenues and estates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts from superiors to inferiors (donations) differ in meaning and lead to salaries/maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Presents bestowed by superiors are given as donations (not offerings) and, as political power centralizes, ruling persons give back part of monopolized wealth to dependents; such donations evolve into salaries and royal bounty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chinese distinction between donations (from superiors) and offerings (from inferiors); medieval liveries and dress‑gifts (Duke of Burgundy, kings) for household officers; Tacitus on Germanic chiefs providing liberality as pay; Dahomey and Kukis where king gives ministers royal bounty; this system leads to remunerative practices and salaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary meaning of presents (signifying obedience) creates ceremonial character of sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally intrinsic propitiatory value of a present can acquire secondary extrinsic meaning as a sign of loyalty/obedience; this secondary meaning gives the ceremonial character to sacrifices that persists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes parallel between presents to visible rulers and invisible rulers (gods): 'the presents to the invisible ruler, primarily considered as directly useful, secondarily come to signify obedience; and their secondary meaning gives that ceremonial character to sacrifice which still survives.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts between non‑related/alien parties may underlie other social actions (e.g., barter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of presents passed between strangers or members of alien societies suggests the question whether propitiatory gifts in these contexts help originate other social actions such as barter; barter is not universally understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentions Cook's failure to exchange with Australians who 'had ... no idea of' barter; invites inquiry into the social origins of reciprocal exchange distinct from hierarchical present‑making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation of present‑making occurs at multiple social levels (political, judicial, ecclesiastical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same process by which presents to supreme rulers become tribute/taxes repeats with subordinate officials (yielding maintenance or bribes) and with ecclesiastical functionaries (forming church incomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross‑societal corroboration: examples from Chibchas, Sumatra, Norman/medieval Europe, Russia, Spain, Peru, Greece, Hebrews, early Christianity. The essay repeatedly generalizes that propitiatory gifts at various levels institutionalize into routine revenue.
